questions.stem: During the Heian period (794–1185), the imperial capital was Heian-kyō. What is this city called today?
options: Kyoto
Tokyo
Osaka
Kamakura
questions.explanation: Heian-kyō, 'capital of peace and tranquillity', was founded in 794 and is today's Kyoto; it remained the emperor's home until 1868. Tokyo grew from Edo, the Tokugawa shoguns' headquarters. Kamakura was the seat of the first shogunate, far to the east.

questions.stem: In feudal Japan, what was a shogun?
options: A lord who ruled a single domain with his own large army of samurai
The supreme military ruler who governed in the emperor's name
The emperor, believed to descend from the sun goddess
The chief Buddhist priest who advised the imperial court
questions.explanation: The shogun was the top military commander, and from 1192 shoguns held the real political power while the emperor in Kyoto kept religious and ceremonial importance. The emperor was never replaced, which is why the shogun ruled in his name. A lord ruling one domain was a daimyo.

questions.stem: Who took the title of shogun in 1192 and set up the first shogunate, at Kamakura?
options: Minamoto no Yoritomo
Tokugawa Ieyasu
Oda Nobunaga
Toyotomi Hideyoshi
questions.explanation: Minamoto no Yoritomo defeated the rival Taira clan in the Genpei War and was named shogun in 1192, ruling from Kamakura. Tokugawa Ieyasu became shogun much later, in 1603. Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi helped unify Japan in the 1500s but never held the title of shogun.

options: Powerful lords who ruled domains and kept their own samurai
Peasant farmers who paid their rice taxes to the samurai
Merchants who grew rich by trading goods in the busy castle towns
Monks who ran Zen Buddhist temples in the mountains
questions.explanation: The daimyo were great landholding lords who controlled domains and commanded their own samurai, owing loyalty to the shogun. Peasants paid rice taxes to them and their samurai. Under the Tokugawa there were roughly 250 to 300 daimyo domains.

questions.stem: In the four-class order set out by Confucian scholars in Tokugawa Japan, which group came just below the samurai?
options: Peasant farmers
Merchants
Artisans
Actors and entertainers
questions.explanation: In this Confucian scheme the order was samurai, then peasants, then artisans, then merchants (historians now debate how strictly it applied in practice), because farmers produced the food everyone depended on. Merchants were ranked lowest even though many became very wealthy, a contradiction that grew during the Edo period. Actors and entertainers were placed outside the four classes altogether.

questions.stem: Which values were most admired in the samurai code later known as bushido?
options: Wealth, luxury and the proud display of fine possessions
Equality between samurai, merchants, artisans and peasant farmers
Peace, trade and friendship with foreign countries
Loyalty to one's lord, honour, courage and self-discipline
questions.explanation: Bushido, 'the way of the warrior', stressed loyalty to one's lord above all, along with honour, courage, frugality and self-control. Samurai were expected to scorn luxury, and the code firmly supported the class hierarchy. The word bushido and its written rules mostly date from the peaceful Edo period, when samurai had become officials as much as fighters.

questions.stem: Under the samurai code, what was seppuku?
options: An oath of loyalty sworn by a samurai to his daimyo before a battle
A ritual suicide a samurai might carry out to avoid disgrace or capture
A formal duel fought with wooden swords to settle a serious question of honour
A ceremony in which a boy received his first sword and became a samurai
questions.explanation: Seppuku was ritual suicide, seen as a way for a samurai to keep his honour rather than face defeat, capture or shame; it could also be ordered as a punishment. It shows how strongly the warrior class valued honour and loyalty. The coming-of-age ceremony and loyalty oaths were separate customs.

questions.stem: What was the Sengoku ('Warring States') period, from the late 1400s to the late 1500s?
options: Hideyoshi's invasions of Korea, which ended soon after his death in 1598
The civil war that ended the Tokugawa shogunate in 1868
A century of war between rival daimyo after the shogunate lost control
The Mongol invasions of Japan, which were turned back by great storms
questions.explanation: After the Onin War (1467–1477) weakened the Ashikaga shoguns, daimyo fought one another for land and power for about a century, building castles and large armies. The Mongol invasions came much earlier, in 1274 and 1281. Hideyoshi's Korean campaigns (1592–1598) came after he had largely unified Japan.

questions.stem: Which order correctly lists the three leaders who unified Japan?
options: Oda Nobunaga, Tokugawa Ieyasu, Toyotomi Hideyoshi
Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, Tokugawa Ieyasu
Toyotomi Hideyoshi, Oda Nobunaga, Tokugawa Ieyasu
Tokugawa Ieyasu, Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi
questions.explanation: Oda Nobunaga began unification until his death in 1582, his general Toyotomi Hideyoshi completed it by 1590, and Tokugawa Ieyasu won power after Hideyoshi's death and founded the long-lasting shogunate. A Japanese saying puts it this way: Nobunaga pounded the rice, Hideyoshi kneaded the rice cake, and Ieyasu ate it.

questions.stem: Victory at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 allowed which leader to become shogun in 1603?
options: Oda Nobunaga
Ashikaga Takauji
Tokugawa Ieyasu
Toyotomi Hideyoshi
questions.explanation: Tokugawa Ieyasu defeated the rival western daimyo at Sekigahara and was appointed shogun in 1603, ruling from Edo. His family held the title until 1867. Ashikaga Takauji had founded the earlier Ashikaga shogunate in the 1300s.

questions.stem: How did the alternate attendance system (sankin-kōtai) help the Tokugawa control the daimyo?
options: Daimyo had to send their samurai to fight in Korea every second year, at their own great cost
Daimyo took turns to act as emperor for a year, keeping each one busy in Kyoto's court
Daimyo lived in Edo every other year and left their families there, which cost them heavily
Daimyo swapped domains with each other every year so they could never build local support
questions.explanation: Daimyo had to spend alternate years in Edo, with their wives and heirs living there permanently as virtual hostages. The huge cost of the processions and two households drained their wealth, leaving less for raising armies against the shogun. The system also spread roads, inns and trade across Japan.

questions.stem: Under the Tokugawa closed-country policy (sakoku), which Europeans were still allowed to trade with Japan, from the small island of Dejima in Nagasaki?
options: The Dutch
The Portuguese
The Spanish
The English
questions.explanation: From 1641 the Dutch East India Company was the only European trader allowed, confined to Dejima, and Chinese merchants also traded at Nagasaki. The Portuguese were expelled in 1639 because they were linked to Catholic missionaries, and the Spanish had been banned earlier. The English had closed their trading post in 1623.

questions.stem: Why did the Tokugawa shoguns adopt the closed-country policy in the 1630s?
options: Europeans had no interest in buying anything that Japan produced
The emperor in Kyoto forbade the shogun to meet or trade with any foreigners at all
A plague carried by European ships had killed most of the people of Edo
They feared Christianity and European influence could weaken loyalty to the shogun
questions.explanation: Christianity had gained many followers, and the shoguns feared converts would be loyal to foreign priests and powers rather than to them; the Shimabara Rebellion of 1637–1638, which involved many Christians, deepened that fear. Japanese people were then banned from travelling abroad, and missionaries were expelled. European traders had been keen to buy Japanese silver.

questions.stem: Heavy logging for castles, temples and cities caused serious deforestation in Japan by the 1600s. How did the Tokugawa respond?
options: They controlled logging strictly and encouraged large-scale replanting of forests
They imported nearly all of their timber from the Dutch traders at Dejima
They banned wooden houses, so all new buildings in the cities had to be made of stone
They moved the capital to a forested island so builders had new trees
questions.explanation: The shogunate and daimyo introduced strict rules on who could cut which trees, kept records of forests and promoted planting, and Japan's forests gradually recovered. Japan never relied on imported timber, and wood remained the main building material. Historians see this as an early example of sustainable resource management.

questions.stem: Why did Zen Buddhism appeal to many samurai?
options: Its meditation and discipline helped warriors stay calm when facing danger and death
It promised that warriors who died bravely in battle would all be reborn as future emperors
It required samurai to give all their land and wealth to the Zen temples
It replaced Shinto as the religion of the emperor and the imperial family
questions.explanation: Zen stressed meditation, self-discipline and acting without fear or hesitation, which suited the life of a warrior, and it shaped arts such as the tea ceremony and garden design. It did not promise rebirth as an emperor. Shinto remained central to the imperial family, and many Japanese followed both Shinto and Buddhism.

options: Japan's native religion, honouring kami (spirits) in nature and ancestors
a form of Buddhism brought to Japan from India by Zen monks
the code of conduct that Tokugawa Ieyasu wrote down for all samurai to obey
a Christian group set up by European missionaries in Nagasaki
questions.explanation: Shinto is Japan's indigenous religion, centred on kami, sacred spirits found in mountains, rivers, trees and ancestors, and the imperial family traced its descent from the sun goddess Amaterasu. Buddhism arrived from the Asian mainland in the 500s and the two religions existed side by side. Christianity arrived only in 1549.

questions.stem: Why is 1853 a turning point in Japanese history?
options: A Mongol fleet attacked Japan and was destroyed by a great typhoon
American warships under Commodore Perry arrived and demanded Japan open its ports
The Dutch traders at Dejima were expelled and all foreign trade with Japan came to an end
British troops landed at Edo and forced the shogun to give up all of his power
questions.explanation: In 1853 Commodore Matthew Perry's steam-powered 'black ships' entered Edo Bay, and in 1854 Japan signed the Treaty of Kanagawa, opening ports to American ships. This ended more than two centuries of strict isolation. The Mongol invasions had come in the 1200s, and British troops never forced the shogun from power.

questions.stem: Which explanation best accounts for the fall of the Tokugawa shogunate in 1867–1868?
options: Peasants overthrew both the emperor and the shogun and then set up a republic in Kyoto
The last shogun died without an heir, so the title passed back to the emperor by law
Unequal treaties with foreign powers made it look weak, and rival domains backed the emperor
Commodore Perry captured Edo, removed the shogun and governed Japan for the United States
questions.explanation: After being forced to sign unequal treaties, the shogunate seemed unable to defend Japan, and powerful domains such as Satsuma and Choshu rallied behind the emperor. The last shogun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, resigned in 1867, and in the Meiji Restoration of 1868 power was returned to the emperor. Perry never occupied Japan, and the monarchy survived.

questions.stem: Which legacy of the Tokugawa period can still be seen in Japan today?
options: Edo, the shogun's capital, became Tokyo, the capital of modern Japan
Japan is still governed by a shogun who rules alongside the emperor
Japanese law still ranks merchants below farmers and craftspeople
Foreign ships are still only allowed to trade at the port of Nagasaki
questions.explanation: Edo grew into one of the largest cities in the world under the Tokugawa and was renamed Tokyo ('eastern capital') in 1868, when the emperor moved there. The shogunate was abolished in the Meiji Restoration, and the class system and trade restrictions were swept away soon after. Many castle towns founded in the period are also still major cities.
